title: DOM Template Refs
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of DOM Template Refs in a Vue 3 application.
Apply at least one of the syllabus subtopics in a small, inspectable example.
Verify one expected behavior and identify a relevant edge case.

content.intro: This lesson studies DOM Template Refs within Component Architecture and Lifecycle. The source PDF subtopics are preserved below and connected to an original working-style example.
content.why_it_matters: Correct lifecycle placement prevents stale DOM assumptions, duplicated subscriptions, and memory leaks.

content_blocks.title: DOM Template Refs: Asynchronous data workflow
content_blocks.alt_text: Asynchronous data workflow diagram for lesson 57: DOM Template Refs. Start the request for the current input → Show pending, success, empty, or failure → Cancel stale work and display useful feedback
content_blocks.caption: Data workflow: model all request states and prevent late or failed responses from silently breaking the interface.

content_blocks.title: The idea in context
content_blocks.text: Lifecycle hooks, template refs, update scheduling, and error capture let components coordinate with the DOM and external systems. This lesson focuses on DOM Template Refs. Start by naming the state, component, browser behavior, or deployment boundary involved; then predict what should change and test the smallest example.

items.title: Referencing DOM elements
items.text: For Referencing DOM elements, identify the reactive source that changes and the value or side effect that depends on it. Prefer computed values for derived data; use watchers when a change must trigger work outside pure derivation, and keep dependencies explicit.

items.title: Accessing child component instances
items.text: For Accessing child component instances, document what data enters the component, which events leave it, and where shared content or behavior belongs. Keep props one-way, emit changes rather than mutating parent-owned values, and add slots only when a real composition point is needed.

items.title: Refs inside v-for
items.text: For Refs inside v-for, identify the reactive source that changes and the value or side effect that depends on it. Prefer computed values for derived data; use watchers when a change must trigger work outside pure derivation, and keep dependencies explicit.

items.title: Conditional and asynchronous elements
items.text: For Conditional and asynchronous elements, model pending, success, empty, and failure states. Check HTTP status before treating a response as success, cancel stale work where appropriate, and do not let a late response overwrite newer user intent.

content_blocks.code:
<script setup>
import { ref, onMounted } from 'vue'
const searchInput = ref(null)
onMounted(() => searchInput.value?.focus())
</script>
<template><label>Search <input ref="searchInput" /></label></template>
content_blocks.expected_output: After mount, focus moves to the input. Ensure this is appropriate for the user flow and does not interrupt other focus management.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Run as App.vue. A template ref is null before the element mounts; avoid reading it during setup as though it already exists.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the initial values or original code, reload the development app/test, and repeat once with a boundary or failure case. Remove temporary logs and test data before committing.

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Work through DOM Template Refs with a predict–change–verify loop. First state the expected UI or console output. Change only the relevant input/state value, then observe the result. Compare it with the expected output in the code block; if it differs, check the exact file, runtime/version, browser Console, and network response before widening the investigation.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Extend the example to include “Accessing child component instances”. Keep the same behavior for the ordinary input, then try an empty, invalid, repeated, or failure condition that makes sense for the example. Record the expected result before testing.

items.title: Assuming behavior instead of checking it
items.text: Write down the expected result and reproduce the issue in the smallest possible example; inspect the browser Console and the exact reactive value or request.

items.title: Ignoring an edge case
items.text: Try empty input, a missing item, repeated interaction, a failed request, or unmounting while work is pending; handle the case explicitly.

items.title: Putting every responsibility in one component
items.text: Separate display, reusable logic, API service, and shared state when that boundary makes the behavior easier to test and explain.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: Remember: Lifecycle hooks, template refs, update scheduling, and error capture let components coordinate with the DOM and external systems. For DOM Template Refs, keep the example small, verify the rendered or logged result, and consult the official references when behavior depends on a specific Vue or ecosystem version.

content_blocks.title: Accessibility, version, and runtime notes
content_blocks.text: Use semantic HTML, readable labels, keyboard-operable controls, and visible errors where the example interacts with users. Vue examples are intended for Vue 3.x with create-vue/Vite unless a legacy or specialist lesson explicitly says otherwise. This CodeLeaf playground does not execute arbitrary Vue code; the snippets are labeled for static validation and should be run in a separate local project.

content.task: Create a small example for “DOM Template Refs” that applies “Referencing DOM elements”, predicts the expected result, and verifies a relevant boundary case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates the named Vue concept rather than only mentioning it.
The expected output or observable behavior is written down and can be checked locally.
At least one boundary, loading, invalid-input, or failure case is tested or explicitly reasoned about.
The example uses semantic/accessible interaction patterns and does not treat frontend state as authoritative security.
hints: Start with the smallest observable part of “Referencing DOM elements”.
Predict the output before changing one input at a time.
Use the browser Console, Vue DevTools, or the appropriate test runner to isolate a mismatch.

common_mistakes.problem: The example only covers the happy path.
common_mistakes.why: Real interfaces receive empty values, delayed responses, invalid input, and failed requests.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one realistic edge/failure case and state its expected behavior.

common_mistakes.problem: The code assumes an API or feature exists in every runtime.
common_mistakes.why: Tool and API support depends on Vue, the build tool, or the chosen SSR/test framework.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the linked official reference and record the runtime/version assumption.

summary: DOM Template Refs belongs to the broader area Component Architecture and Lifecycle.
The main concept to practice is Referencing DOM elements.
Verify a normal result and one meaningful boundary case before using the pattern in a production feature.
